headline: High: Great Expectations can read and write shared files while awesome-prompts can shape instructions, creating default-path prompt-injection and data-handling risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-prompts is a prompt-writing/content source, and great_expectations reads and writes files in its workspace. If prompt text or generated instructions are placed in shared files, B can ingest attacker-controlled content from A as trusted input. No direct shared-channel proof is present, so I choose medium rather than low because the file bridge is explicit in B and A is instruction content.
conditions: IF agent_a outputs prompt text into a file that agent_b later parses as instructions
IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace directory
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories
Treat A-produced files as untrusted input in B
Add a manual review step before B consumes A outputs
Use read-only mounts for A outputs
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between file producers and consumers

B_data_leakage.rationale: B explicitly touches data sources, validation results, and documentation via files, while A is a content-writing/prompt repository with no network egress. Shared workspace use could expose B's validation artifacts to A-generated content or vice versa. The pair does not show secrets handling or external upload, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF agent_b stores validation results in a directory readable by agent_a
IF either agent is run on the same filesystem workspace
mitigations: Use separate workspaces per agent
Restrict file permissions on validation outputs
Keep sensitive validation artifacts out of shared folders
Review generated docs before publishing
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation in the orchestrator

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has no write or network capabilities exposed, while B can install packages and write files. There is no evidence that A can mutate shared state, so direct write-write conflict is limited. The only plausible conflict is if both are manually pointed at the same files, which is unusual and small in blast radius.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to modify the same directory
IF B installs packages into an environment A also depends on
mitigations: Pin B to a dedicated environment
Avoid shared writable directories
Run package installs in an isolated venv
Lock shared files during edits
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level resource locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: A produces prompt/content material and B produces validation results and documentation. If B treats A's generated text as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into published docs or tests. Because B is a data-engineering tool that can operationalize inputs, the pathway exists in default workflows, though not proven to be automatic.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated text as source material for documentation or tests
IF B does not verify claims before emitting results
mitigations: Require human review of A-derived inputs
Add validation checks before B publishes outputs
Mark A content as draft-only
Compare B outputs against source data
requires-engineering: add automated provenance and verification gates

E_compliance.rationale: A is an open-source prompt repository with no touched regulated data classes, while B handles data quality tests, validation results, and documentation. No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented, so compliance risk is limited to ordinary documentation handling. I do not cite only one agent because the issue is the pair's combined data flow, but the evidence is sparse.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into B's validation inputs
IF B's documentation includes jurisdiction-bound personal data
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of validation docs
Review retention settings for generated artifacts
Redact sensitive fields before testing
Document data-class boundaries
requires-engineering: add residency and retention policy enforcement
